title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people for the time of day, introduce yourself, and say who you are.

dialogs.title: Diálogo — En la escuela de idiomas
dialogs.intro: Two strangers meet in the hallway of a language school. Read the Spanish out loud first, then glance at the translation.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.id: I'm Luis. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: Nice to meet you too. Are you a student?

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.text: Sí, soy estudiante. Y tú, ¿eres profesora?
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you, are you a teacher?
lines.literal: yes, am student. and you, you-are teacher?

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: No, no soy profesora. Soy estudiante también.
lines.id: No, I'm not a teacher. I'm a student too.
lines.literal: no, not am teacher. am student also.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Muy bien, gracias. Un poco cansada, pero bien.
lines.id: Very well, thanks. A little tired, but fine.
lines.literal: very well, thanks. a little tired, but well.

lines.speaker: Luis:
lines.id: Oh, great! See you later, Ana.
lines.literal: ah, very well! until later, Ana.

notes: **Pronouns can be dropped.** *Soy estudiante* already means "I'm a student" without *yo*, because the verb form itself shows who is speaking. *Yo* is used for emphasis: *Yo soy Luis* = "as for **me**, I'm Luis". That's why Spanish sounds so economical — half of its pronouns are never actually said.

**Double question and exclamation marks.** Spanish opens a question with ¿ and an exclamation with ¡. It's practical: the reader knows the tone of the sentence from the start, not only at the end. On a phone, these marks appear when you long-press ? or !.

**Encantado / encantada.** It means "nice to meet you", but its form follows the gender of the **speaker**: a man says *encantado*, a woman *encantada*. The same thing happens with *cansado / cansada* in line 9 — Ana is a woman, so she's *cansada*. *Mucho gusto* is safe for anyone because it isn't an adjective.

**Saying no is easy.** Just put *no* in front of the verb: *soy* → *no soy*. When answering a question, *no* appears twice: *No, no soy profesora* — the first means "no", the second is part of the sentence. There's no helper verb like English "do".

**Buenos días** is used until around noon, then *buenas tardes* until sunset, and *buenas noches* after that. Notice: *días* is plural, so the adjective is plural too — *buenos*. And *buenas noches* works both as a greeting and as "good night" before bed.

**¿Cómo estás? doesn't use *ser*.** How you are and how you feel use a different verb, *estar*, which is covered in Unit 11. For now, learn it as one whole phrase: *¿cómo estás?* (informal) and *¿cómo está usted?* (polite).
**Un poco** = "a little", always before the adjective: *un poco cansada*, *un poco difícil*. Don't flip it.

grammars.title: The verb ser (to be) — the first three forms
body: *Ser* is used for **identity** — who you are, what you do, where you're from, what you're like. Its form changes with the person, and these three forms are all you need for this unit:
after: Look at the last row: *usted* (polite "you") uses exactly the same form as *él / ella*. Strange at first, but it makes sense once you know where it comes from — *usted* was once *vuestra merced*, "Your Grace", and people spoke about it in the third person rather than addressing it directly.

The most basic identity sentence is **A es B**, with nothing in between: *Ana es profesora*, *yo soy estudiante*. And unlike English, jobs take no article — not *soy una profesora*, but *soy profesora*.

blocks.text: Answering *¿qué tal?* doesn't need to be long: *bien, gracias* is enough, and it's almost always followed by *¿y tú?* — returning the question is polite; leaving it hanging sounds cold.
